q: What does the FDIC tell borrowers about making their loan payments after their bank fails?
answer:
The FDIC tells borrowers after their bank fails that:

- The FDIC sends written notice with payment instructions and points-of-contact to borrowers whose loans it has retained.
- Borrowers are strongly encouraged to seek a new lender to refinance their loan and serve as a replacement source of funding.
- The FDIC may offer incentives to refinance by offsetting some or all of the associated closing costs.
- The FDIC will offset borrowers' outstanding loan balances against the uninsured deposit balance of the same borrower if certain parameters are met.
- A bank failure does not change the borrower's obligation to make payments and comply with the loan terms.
- If the FDIC sells the loan, the borrower will receive a notice with payment mailing instructions from the FDIC or the new owner.
- The sale does not affect the terms of the loan, and the new owner must comply with all applicable laws and is entitled to collect all amounts owed.

(Source: FDIC · A Borrower's Guide to an FDIC-Insured Bank Failure, p.1, https://www.fdic.gov/bank-failures/borrowers-guide-fdic-insured-bank-failure)

q: According to the FDIC's history of the crisis, how fast did acquisition, development and construction lending grow from 1996 to 2006?
answer:
Acquisition, development, and construction (ADC) lending grew especially fast from 1996 to 2006, at an annualized rate of nearly 19 percent for the ten-year period. 

Additional points:
- During this decade, nominal GDP grew at an annualized rate of 5.4 percent.
- Loans outstanding at FDIC-insured institutions grew at an annualized rate of 7.5 percent.
- The rapid growth of ADC loans was a notable feature of the banking conditions leading up to the crisis.
- This growth in ADC lending was part of a broader trend of rapid increases in home prices and real estate lending during that period.

Source: "acquisition, development, and construction [ADC] lending grew especially fast, at an annualized rate of nearly 19 percent for the ten-year" (Crisis and Response: An FDIC History, 2008-2013 · Ch. 4 Bank Supervision · Banking Conditions, p.6) https://www.fdic.gov/resources/publications/crisis-response/book/crisis-response-chapter-4.pdf

q: Among the 2008-2012 failures, which balance-sheet traits went with the costliest failures?
answer:
Among the 2008-2012 failed banks, the balance-sheet traits that were associated with the costliest failures (top-third loss rate) include:

- High construction & land development loans combined with low equity capital/assets, found in 24 banks, with a confidence of 71% and a lift of 2.12, indicating a strong association with costly failure.
- High construction & land development loans combined with high noncurrent loans/loans, found in 56 banks, with a confidence of 64% and a lift of 1.92.
- High brokered deposits (share of deposits) combined with high noncurrent loans/loans, found in 28 banks, with a confidence of 61% and a lift of 1.81.

Other traits such as high construction & land development loans alone, low equity capital/assets combined with high noncurrent loans/loans, and high loans/assets combined with high noncurrent loans/loans also appear but with lifts below the threshold for strong association.

These findings indicate that banks with large shares of construction and land development loans, especially when paired with weak capital or high noncurrent loans, tended to have the costliest failures (Loan Desk analysis of FDIC failures and Call Report data, 2008-2012).

q: What is a shared-loss purchase and assumption?
answer:
A shared-loss purchase and assumption (P&A) is a resolution method where the FDIC, as receiver, agrees to share losses with the assuming institution (AI) on certain types of loans. This arrangement is used to facilitate the sale of loans that might otherwise not be sold to an acquirer at the time of resolution. The FDIC typically absorbs a significant portion of future credit losses on designated shared loss assets for a specific period. The rationale is that keeping these assets in the banking sector yields a better net recovery for the FDIC than liquidating them.

Key points:
- It is similar to a whole bank P&A but includes loss sharing on certain assets up to a limit.
- It minimizes disruptions to customers and conserves FDIC cash.
- Shared loss reduces the FDIC's immediate cash needs and moves assets quickly back to the private sector.
- The assuming institution accepts a portion of credit losses (e.g., 20% or more during the recent financial crisis).
- Shared loss assets often include residential loans, commercial loans, and real estate.
- It requires additional administrative duties and governance to manage shared loss assets.
- Some bidders may find the added duties unacceptable, so other resolution methods are offered simultaneously.

Source: (FDIC Resolutions Handbook, pp. 22, 31) "Shared Loss - A method in a Purchase and Assumption (P&A) transaction in which the FDIC as receiver agrees to share losses with the assuming institution (AI) on certain types of loans... The FDIC usually agrees to absorb a significant portion of future credit losses on assets that have been designated as shared loss assets for a specific period of time." and "A P&A with Shared Loss is similar to a Whole Bank P&A transaction, except that the FDIC as receiver agrees to share losses on certain types of assets (up to an established limit)..."

q: Under the handbook, what does the least cost test require?
answer:
The least cost test (LCT) requires the FDIC to compare the cost of liquidating the failing insured depository institution to the cost of all bids received for its resolution. The FDIC must choose the resolution alternative that represents the least cost to the Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF). This involves evaluating all possible resolution alternatives and computing costs on a net present value basis. If liquidation is the least costly option, the FDIC pays insured depositors up to the deposit insurance limits and liquidates the assets of the failed institution. If an acceptable least cost bid is received, the FDIC transfers deposits and assets to the assuming institution according to the purchase and assumption agreement.

Key points:
- The FDIC compares liquidation cost to bid costs to determine the least costly resolution.
- Costs are evaluated on a net present value basis.
- Factors considered include asset and liability book values, insured and uninsured deposits, premiums paid by assuming institutions, losses on contingent claims, realized liquidation values, and recoveries from affiliated institutions.
- If liquidation is least costly, the FDIC pays insured depositors and liquidates assets.
- If a least cost bid is accepted, deposits and assets are transferred to the assuming institution.

Source: (FDIC Resolutions Handbook, pp. 10, 12)
